newsitem.title: PERU: Tokyo official arrives in Lima to discuss hostages.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo official arrives in Lima to discuss hostages.

text.p: A top Tokyo official arrived in Peru on Tuesday on the first leg of a three-nation tour aimed at finding a peaceful solution to the standoff with Marxist rebels holding 72 VIP hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.

In a sign of its impatience at the 91-day siege, Japan sent its Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura to discuss the crisis despite having its Mexican ambassador, Terusuke Tarada, based in Lima as a point man observing negotiations.

Komura landed about 0030 local time (0530 GMT) amid tight police security and was accompanied by several more officials and a score of Japanese journalists. He did not speak to local journalists waiting for his arrival at the international airport in Lima's port of Callao.
Throughout the three-month-old crisis, Japan has shown a willingness to promote dialogue with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) and has aimed to quiet Peru's more hawkish stretegies.

It is no surprise, then, that only the second visit to Lima by a Japanese government official during the crisis coincides with a break in talks and follows rebel accusations that Peru built a tunnel under the residence for a planned attack.

A spokesman at Lima's Government Palace said the Komura was slated to meet with Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori at 1030 local (1500 GMT). He was also due to meet relatives of the 20-odd Japanese hostages later on Tuesday before leaving Peru on Wednesday.
Komura was then expected to fly to Cuba and the Dominican Republic to seek cooperation in arranging asylum for the Cuban-inspired rebels should they agree to leave Peru.
Diplomatic sources in Santo Domingo said Komura would travel to Havana after leaving Lima and meet at noon Thursday with Dominican leader Leonel Fernandez.
In early March, Fujimori made a surprise trip to Havana to meet Cuban President Fidel Castro in Havana, after which the communist leader said he was willing to accept the rebels.

A three-man guarantors commission has been exploring possible ways of making tangible progress in negotiations after 10 rounds of face-to-face meetings resulted in little more than both sides politely exchanging their divergent positions.

They shuttled between meetings Tuesday with the rebels and government in an effort to unblock the stalled talks. But after four hours of discussions they could not offer the prospect of fresh negotiations.

Government negotiator Domingo Palermo told reporters he did not know when Latin America's longest hostage siege would end. "These matters unfortunately take an indeterminate amount of time," he said. "Nobody can fix a time limit for such a delicate subject."
Peruvians vented their frustration with the lack of progress, banging pots, ringing church bells and sounding car horns in a nationwide demonstration to demand the hostages be freed.
More than 500 captives were taken on Dec. 17, 1996, when about 20 jungle-trained rebels blew a hole in the residence's outer wall and swarmed into the building in a fierce shootout.
But the MRTA gradually released most of its hostages, keeping those it considered most valuable as bargaining chips to demand the freedom of some 400 jailed comrades.
